Description: Why quads struggle outdoors: built for flat, very smooth indoor floors. A certified coach says skating quads outdoors is significantly harder, and very possible: rough ground easily catches the wide, flat wheel profile and the short wheelbase. Title: On Quads Outdoors, the Fall to Watch Is Backwards
Description: Why beginners on quads tip over backwards far more easily outdoors: a very short wheelbase, the front-to-back distance between the wheels, says a certified coach, and outdoor bumps make posture slip. The answer is the same on every skate: knees bent, weight forward over the front of the foot, never upright. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: A Quad Heel Is Already Raised. Bend Your Knees Anyway
Description: Most classic quad boots have a slightly raised heel, which pushes your weight forward onto the balls of your feet by itself. A certified coach counts it as an advantage, with one condition: the knee bend is still crucial. Outdoors, where a crack can pitch you back, the raised heel helps but never replaces bent knees. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Quads Steer Through the Trucks, So Outdoor Turns Are Whole-Body Moves
Description: How quads steer outdoors, unlike inline skates' edge changes. Quads turn by pressing into the trucks until they pivot, and a certified coach says that takes more pronounced knee and body movement. Outside, where a turn is often how you avoid a hole or a pedestrian, expect quad steering to be deliberate and big rather than subtle. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: On Quads, Take the Shortest Line Across Bad Ground
Description: How to cross cobbles and broken tarmac on quads: take the shortest line. A certified coach's first rule: gain as much momentum as you can on the smooth part, then angle your line to cross the rough section by the most direct path, so you spend the least time on bad ground. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby, taught to inline and quad beginners. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: A Small Hip Bounce Keeps Quad Wheels Out of the Gaps
Description: Keeping quad wheels out of gaps. A certified coach's fix for rough ground: drop into a deep scissor stance, one skate ahead, knees over toes, and add a subtle, continuous bounce from the hips. It keeps your weight light over the front wheels so they skim the holes instead of dropping in. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby, taught for inline and quad skates. Title: Uphill on Quads: Short, Quick Steps, or Gravity Wins Between Them
Description: How to climb a hill on quads: short, quick steps, not long, wide pushes. A certified coach explains why they fail: every long push gives gravity time to pull you back down between steps. Switch to a high-cadence stride, short and rapid, so the momentum never drops. The rule is taught to quad and inline skaters alike. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Skating Uphill: Land Your Heels on an Imaginary Centre Line
Description: How to set your skates down on a climb: a wide gap between your feet makes the stance unstable and kills your energy. A certified coach's cue for quad and inline skaters: imagine a centre line running up the slope and set every skate down so the heel lands right on it. Narrow, short, quick, and the climb no longer drains you. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
